title: AI Fluency for Educators (Anthropic Academy)
author: Anthropic, with Prof. Rick Dakan (Ringling College) and Prof. Joseph Feller (University College Cork)
summary: Four lessons that apply the 4D framework (Delegation, Description, Discernment, Diligence) to course design, learning outcomes, lesson materials and assignments. It teaches a way of working with any AI chat tool, not a set of Claude buttons.
who_for: University lecturers and instructional designers, for their own work. Also works for senior-school teachers who plan whole courses rather than single lessons.
skip_if: Skip if you have never opened an AI chat tool - it assumes the 4D framework from the Framework and Foundations course. Skip if you want Claude-specific, click-by-click steps; this is deliberately model-agnostic.
notes: Free, but you must make a Skilljar account, which is separate from your Claude login. Runs about 3 hours including roughly 35 minutes of video - that length is stated on aifluencyframework.org, not on the course page itself. Materials are CC BY-NC-SA, so a department can adapt them.

title: Teaching AI Fluency (Anthropic Academy)
author: Anthropic, with Prof. Rick Dakan (Ringling College) and Prof. Joseph Feller (University College Cork)
summary: Seven lessons on how to teach and assess AI fluency in your own subject: the Delegation-Diligence and Description-Discernment loops, how to assess the 4Ds, and how to design assignments that still measure student thinking.
who_for: University lecturers and school teachers whose job is to teach students about AI, not only to use it themselves. The assignment-design and assessment lessons are the strongest part.
skip_if: Skip if you only want to cut your own marking and planning time - this is curriculum and assessment work. Skip if you have not done Framework and Foundations first; it assumes the 4Ds.
notes: About 5-6 hours including roughly 70 minutes of video (length taken from aifluencyframework.org). CC BY-NC-SA licensed, so slides and exercises can be re-used for staff training. Needs a Skilljar account.

title: AI Fluency for pK-12 Educators
author: Anthropic with Teach For America
summary: The school-level version of the AI fluency course: how AI works and where it fails, the 4D framework, getting better outputs, ethics and responsible use, ending with a quiz and a certificate.
who_for: School (pK-12) teachers and support staff who are new to AI and want their own practice covered first. Built around real school constraints - limited budget, many people to answer to.
skip_if: Skip if you already use AI daily; the first half is beginner material. Skip if you want ready-made classroom prompts - this teaches judgement, not a prompt pack.
notes: Model-agnostic; examples use Claude.ai. The page gives no duration - ten short lessons plus a quiz, so half a day is my estimate, not a published figure. Benjamin Riley has publicly criticised one quiz item for putting FERPA compliance on individual teachers rather than on districts.

title: AI Fluency for pK-12 Train the Trainer
author: Anthropic with the American Federation of Teachers
summary: A ready-to-run staff workshop kit - slide deck, facilitator guide, grade-band exercises and a learner workbook - so one teacher can lead 4D framework training for colleagues in their own school.
who_for: School AI leads, instructional coaches and heads of department who must deliver INSET or professional development to other teachers.
skip_if: Skip if you will never train other adults. Skip if you have not done the pK-12 Educators course first - the kit assumes you can already answer teachers' questions without notes.
notes: The course itself is short (four items); the value is the downloadable kit, not the lessons. No duration stated on the page. Co-branded with the AFT, so the privacy and policy framing is US-centric.

title: AI Fluency for Students (Anthropic Academy)
author: Anthropic, with Prof. Rick Dakan and Prof. Joseph Feller
summary: Five lessons that apply the 4Ds to a student's own learning and career planning, and end with the student writing a personal policy for responsible AI use.
who_for: University lecturers and senior-school teachers who need something honest to assign instead of building an AI-literacy unit from nothing. Teaching-students, not own work.
skip_if: Skip if your students are under 18 and you need age-appropriate classroom activities - this is written for adult learners and Claude is 18-plus. Skip if you want graded worksheets and a scheme of work.
notes: About 3 hours including roughly 30 minutes of video (length from aifluencyframework.org). CC BY-NC-SA, so you can adapt it for your cohort. This is the Anthropic Academy version, not the Coursera listing of the same name.

title: The AI Fluency Framework - open educational resources hub
author: Prof. Rick Dakan (Ringling College of Art and Design) and Prof. Joseph Feller (University College Cork)
summary: The authors' own index of the 4D framework and of every free course built on it, with lesson counts, running times, licence terms and links to both the Anthropic Academy and OpenCourses.ie versions.
who_for: Any teacher, school or university, who wants to decide which of the four AI Fluency courses to take before creating yet another account.
skip_if: Skip if you already know which course you want - this page is a map, not training. It contains no Claude-specific instructions at all.
notes: The only place that states the actual course lengths, which the Skilljar pages omit. Everything is CC BY-NC-SA. Page copyright reads 2025, so check the course list is still complete before you quote it.

title: Introducing Claude for Teachers
author: Anthropic
summary: The launch announcement: free premium Claude for verified US K-12 school staff, built-in lesson-planning and differentiation skills, a Learning Commons connector carrying academic standards for all 50 states, and K-12 terms written around FERPA.
who_for: US school teachers deciding whether to sign up, and school leaders who need to know exactly what the free offer contains. Own work.
skip_if: Skip if you teach outside the US or in higher education - you are not eligible. Skip if you want a how-to; this is an announcement, and it only shows the workflow that works.
notes: Vendor marketing, but unusually specific: it links the open-source skills repository, the privacy terms and the AI fluency courses. Updated 2026-07-21 to add that district and state policy, not Anthropic, decides what educational data may be used. Read a critic alongside it.

title: Getting started with Claude for Teachers
author: Anthropic
summary: The practical page: who is eligible, how the Goodstack verification works, what the educator plan includes, and four starting prompts for planning, differentiating, building an assessment and drafting family emails.
who_for: US K-12 teachers and school staff who are about to sign up and want the rules before they start. Own work, school level.
skip_if: Skip if you are not US K-12 - the page says plainly that international educators and universities are not eligible. Skip if you are already verified; there is nothing new for you.
notes: Free to read, no login. It answers the questions teachers actually ask: personal email addresses are refused, students cannot have accounts, and you must re-verify periodically. No publication date shown on the page, and the plan details will drift.

title: Claude for Teachers in action - two classroom workflows
author: Anthropic
summary: Two short films of practising teachers: a high-school teacher turning one folder of scores, attendance and notes into a differentiated lesson, and an elementary teacher who has Claude review each day's recorded lesson at 4pm and draft tomorrow's plan.
who_for: School teachers who want to see the workflow end to end before spending time on it. Own work.
skip_if: Skip if your school forbids uploading class data - both examples depend on it. Skip if you have no lesson-recording tool; the second workflow is built on a TeachFX recording. Skip if you want step-by-step instructions rather than demos.
notes: Anthropic-produced marketing films, so they show only the version that works. Videos are hosted on YouTube (IDs sMh99UfkvL4 and V-OOEC5RNaQ). No publication date given on the page. I read the page and video descriptions, not the full videos.

title: Claude for K-12 teachers - product page with worked prompts
author: Anthropic
summary: A sales page worth reading for one reason: it prints five complete prompts next to the finished output, including an NGSS-aligned photosynthesis assessment with a full answer key and a brief on the three common fraction-multiplication misconceptions.
who_for: School teachers who learn faster from a finished example than from instructions, and who want to see what 'good' output looks like before writing their own prompt. Own work.
skip_if: Skip if sales pages irritate you - most of this is claims, logos and testimonials. Skip if you are outside the US, because the free plan is US-only.
notes: This is vendor marketing wearing a teacher costume, and I am saying so plainly. The prompt-and-output examples are real and copyable; the rest is a pitch. Connector list (Brisk, Canva, Diffit, MagicSchool, Eedi, TeachFX) will change.

title: Claude for Teachers: your data and our terms
author: Anthropic Help Center
summary: Plain-English version of the US K-12 terms: no model training on your conversations, you are the data controller and Anthropic the processor, encryption and deletion details, and which Team features are switched off for educators.
who_for: US school teachers and school leaders who must answer 'is this safe for student data?' before anyone in the building signs up.
skip_if: Skip if your district already has its own written agreement with Anthropic - that agreement overrides these terms. Skip if you are outside the US; none of this applies to you.
notes: This is Anthropic's own account of its own terms. Independent critics argue the FERPA position is weaker than it sounds, because an individual teacher cannot designate a vendor as a 'school official' - read Joe Phillips' district piece next to it.

title: Agent Skills for K-12 Teachers (open source)
author: Anthropic with Learning Commons
summary: The source of the two skills that ship with Claude for Teachers - k12-lesson-planning and k12-lesson-differentiation - plus the evaluation rubrics Anthropic used to judge them, packaged as a Claude Code plugin.
who_for: Teachers outside the US who cannot get the official plan, and anyone who wants to read and edit the exact instructions Claude follows when it writes a lesson plan.
skip_if: Skip if you do not use a terminal - installing needs git and Claude Code. Skip if you already have Claude for Teachers, where the skills are installed for you.
notes: Apache-2.0. The skills are written to call the Learning Commons connector, which only verified US teachers get, so output will be weaker without it - the README says to adapt them. One commit and 57 stars when I checked, so it is new and lightly used.

title: Anthropic Education Report: how educators use Claude
author: Anthropic (with Northeastern University faculty interviews)
summary: Analysis of about 74,000 higher-education Claude conversations plus interviews with 22 Northeastern faculty, showing curriculum development is by far the largest use (around 57%), then academic research, then assessing student work.
who_for: University lecturers and teaching-centre staff who want evidence on what colleagues really do with Claude, rather than what a vendor says they should.
skip_if: Skip if you teach at school level - the sample is higher education only. Skip if you want instructions; this is a usage study with no how-to in it.
notes: Anthropic analysing its own product, so read the framing carefully. Published August 2025, which is over twelve months old - it predates Cowork, Skills and Claude for Teachers, so the feature picture is stale even if the task mix is not. Metadata and summaries only; I did not read the full report.

title: Use Claude for Education at your university
author: Anthropic Help Center
summary: The FAQ for a university-sponsored Claude account: what the plan includes, how to sign in on each device, where projects and artifacts live, SSO and usage-limit troubleshooting, and what to do if you already had a personal account on your university email.
who_for: University lecturers and professional staff whose institution has bought Claude for Education. Own work.
skip_if: Skip if your university has no Claude for Education licence - none of it applies. Skip if you want teaching advice; the 'what can I use Claude for' list is written for students, not for people who set assignments.
notes: Dated 13 July 2026, so it is current. It is IT documentation - there is nothing here about pedagogy, assessment or academic integrity beyond a one-line warning.

title: Practical ways to get started using Claude for educators
author: A.J. Juliani
summary: A first-prompt routine that makes Claude interview you about your role before you ask it for anything, then a walk through Projects and Artifacts, ending in an AI-compatible versus AI-resistant decision matrix for engagement, rigour and scaffolding.
who_for: School teachers and school leaders starting from zero. Covers both own work and the harder question of which thinking students must still do without help.
skip_if: Skip if you already use Projects - the first half is beginner material. Skip if you need subject-specific worked examples; the prompts are generic across subjects.
notes: Juliani sells courses and cohorts and the page pushes his newsletter hard, so treat it as marketing-adjacent - but the embedded decision matrix is free, concrete and stands on its own. Screenshots are from February 2026, so the interface has already moved.

title: The Ultimate Claude Guide for Teachers
author: Paul Matthews (Wise AI for Educators)
summary: A switching guide for teachers coming from ChatGPT: what changes, how to set up memory and Projects, five low-risk starting tasks, and a blunt section on hallucinations, data discipline and not outsourcing your own professional thinking.
who_for: School teachers, especially heads of department, who already use ChatGPT and want to know whether Claude is worth the move. Own work.
skip_if: Skip if you have never used any AI tool - it assumes you can already write a prompt. Skip if you need US policy detail; the author writes from an Australian independent school.
notes: Written by a practising head of department and honest about its own AI use. The model names and prices quoted (Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.6, Pro at US$20 a month) were right in April 2026 and will go stale fast - check claude.com/pricing instead.

title: Claude AI for Teachers - the practical guide
author: Patrick Araya (Learning Claude)
summary: A special-education teacher's working stack: one Teaching Project set up once, a small prompt library kept inside it, and five jobs worth learning first - differentiation, IEP target drafting, the hard parent email, whole-class feedback from samples, and rewriting documents into plain English for parents.
who_for: School teachers, especially special-education and inclusion staff, who want a repeatable routine rather than a list of tools. Own work.
skip_if: Skip if you want evidence - the time-saved figures (about five hours a week on planning) are the author's own claim with nothing behind them. Skip if you need US terminology; it uses Year 7, EAL and scheme of work.
notes: The site exists to grow a newsletter and a YouTube channel and every section links deeper into it, so the funnel is obvious. The advice is still sound and the 'anonymise before you paste' rule is stated clearly. No publication date anywhere on the page.

title: 43 Claude Skills for college teachers
author: Doan Winkel (How to Teach With AI)
summary: A catalogue of reusable Claude Skills for the work that repeats every semester - course design, materials, rubrics, rubric-aligned feedback, AI-use policy - built on the argument that you should encode your course once rather than re-prompt every week.
who_for: University lecturers who already use Claude confidently and now want to stop repeating themselves. Own work.
skip_if: Skip if you do not yet know what a Skill is - it does not teach the basics. Skip if you teach at school level; the framing is semesters, syllabi and departments.
notes: Substack with a paid tier, so part of the list may sit behind the paywall. I read the preview and metadata only, not all 43 entries. Treat any grading-time claim with care - LLM grading is inconsistent between identical submissions.

title: Why is Claude for Teachers? (critical hands-on review)
author: Benjamin Riley (Cognitive Resonance)
summary: A hostile hands-on review: the teacher product is one pre-set prompt on top of ordinary Claude, verification wants photos of your staff ID, Anthropic invites teachers to upload rosters and diagnostics, top-model access is cut off after three days, and the AI fluency quiz puts FERPA compliance on individual teachers.
who_for: School teachers and district leaders who need the counter-argument in their hands before they sign a school up. Policy and judgement, not classroom practice.
skip_if: Skip if you want a how-to - there is none here. Skip if the sarcastic tone will stop you seeing the fair points underneath it.
notes: Riley runs a think tank that is openly sceptical of generative AI in schools, so the framing is adversarial by design. His specific claims - the single pre-baked prompt, the Fable cut-off, the FERPA quiz item, the Learning Commons standards graph - are all checkable, which is why this is worth reading.

title: Anthropic launched Claude for Teachers. We blocked it for our district.
author: Dr. Joe Phillips
summary: A district technology officer sets out why his district blocked Claude for Teachers: FERPA lets a vendor act as a 'school official' only where the district designates it and keeps direct control, and an individual teacher cannot make that designation on the district's behalf.
who_for: US school and district leaders deciding whether to allow, block or renegotiate Claude for Teachers. Policy, not classroom practice.
skip_if: Skip if you are a classroom teacher with no say in procurement - it will worry you without giving you an action. Skip if you are outside the US; FERPA does not apply to you.
notes: One district's legal reading, not a ruling, and other districts have reached the opposite conclusion. I found it through Benjamin Riley's 27 July update and have not read it end to end - metadata and summaries only.

title: How to set up a Claude Project that answers questions about your class
author: Hasnain Sikora, Northeastern University Center for Advancing Teaching and Learning Through Research
summary: A step-by-step build of a course FAQ assistant in Claude Projects, with five ready-to-paste system-instruction blocks (due dates, grading policy, weekly readings, course policies, general FAQs) and the exact documents to upload for each one.
who_for: University lecturers who want to cut repeated admin questions and give students a 24-hour answer. Own work with a student-facing result.
skip_if: Skip if your syllabus changes often - the guide itself admits the assistant goes stale the moment the course does. Skip if you teach school; it assumes a syllabus, TAs and a Canvas-style platform.
notes: Published July 2025 and last updated August 2025, so over twelve months old and Projects has changed since - the screenshots and menu names will not match. The system-instruction blocks are the durable part and still work. Written by a student, published by the university teaching centre.

title: AI in assignment design - Cornell Center for Teaching Innovation
author: Cornell University Center for Teaching Innovation
summary: A teaching centre's guidance on redesigning coursework for a world with generative AI: say clearly in the syllabus if and how AI may be used, make student thinking visible, and use AI-written text as material for error analysis rather than only banning it.
who_for: University lecturers rewriting assignments so that a grade still means what it claims to mean. Teaching-students side, not own productivity.
skip_if: Skip if you want Claude-specific instructions - this is tool-neutral pedagogy and never names a product. Skip if you teach school; the examples assume semester-length US higher-education courses.
notes: Metadata and search summaries only; I did not read the whole page. No publication or review date is shown, which matters for AI guidance. Cornell is a credible teaching centre with nothing to sell.

title: The AI Assessment Scale (AIAS)
author: Mike Perkins, Jasper Roe, Leon Furze and Jason MacVaugh
summary: A five-level scale, from no AI to full AI exploration, that gives staff and students one shared vocabulary for how much AI is allowed in a given task, with the peer-reviewed papers and revisions behind it.
who_for: University lecturers and senior-school teachers writing an assessment policy or a per-assignment AI rule. Teaching-students.
skip_if: Skip if you are looking for a way to catch cheating - the scale is about designing tasks, not policing them, and it deliberately refuses to name a 'best' level. Skip if you need K-12 examples; adoption so far is mostly higher education.
notes: Independent academics with published papers behind the scale, revised twice (version 2 and 2.1) since 2023. I checked the site listing and the papers through search results, not the full site. Undated on the landing page, so confirm which version you are looking at.

title: Guidance on AI detection, and why we're disabling Turnitin's AI detector
author: Vanderbilt University (Brightspace / Center for Teaching)
summary: A university's public explanation for switching off Turnitin's AI detector: at its own submission volume the false-positive rate would have wrongly flagged thousands of papers a year, and Turnitin would not explain how the score is produced.
who_for: Teachers and heads of department at any level who are being pushed to adopt an AI detector and need a credible institution's reasoning to point at.
skip_if: Skip if you want current accuracy numbers - this is from August 2023 and the figures have moved since. Skip if you want an alternative to detection; it does not give you one. And never treat any detector score as proof against a student - false accusations fall hardest on non-native English writers.
notes: Nearly three years old, so treat the specifics as history - but it remains the most-cited institutional decision on AI detection, and Cornell, Pittsburgh and others followed. Included here mainly as the counterweight to vendor content that sells detectors as the answer to AI in assignments.

title: Using AI in education settings: support materials (UK DfE)
author: UK Department for Education, with Chiltern Learning Trust and the Chartered College of Teaching
summary: Four free training modules for all school and college staff - understanding AI, interacting with generative AI, safe use, and use cases - plus a separate pack for leaders, each with slides, video, transcripts, knowledge checks and planning templates.
who_for: School and college staff in England, either as whole-staff CPD or as self-study. Own work and school policy, school level.
skip_if: Skip if you are outside England - the safeguarding, data and KCSIE references are UK-specific. Skip if you want tool training; it is deliberately generic and never mentions Claude.
notes: First published 10 June 2025 and updated 19 May 2026 for the 2026/27 academic year, so it is current - I confirmed both dates on the page. Module 3 (safe use) is the one everyone should do regardless of experience. A free certified assessment carrying Chartered Teacher Status credits is available from the Chartered College.

title: The Australian Framework for Generative AI in Schools
author: Australian Government Department of Education, National AI in Schools Taskforce
summary: Six principles and twenty-five guiding statements agreed by all Australian education ministers, covering teaching and learning, human and social wellbeing, transparency, fairness, accountability and privacy in school use of generative AI.
who_for: School leaders and teachers writing a school AI policy - in Australia, or anywhere that wants a short, government-endorsed model to copy.
skip_if: Skip if you want classroom activities; it is a policy framework with no lesson material in it. Skip if you need legal certainty - each state and territory applies it differently.
notes: Approved by education ministers on 5 October 2023, reviewed in 2024, and the review endorsed in June 2025 - so make sure you are reading the reviewed version, not the original. I saw the page in search results and did not open it, so the exact date on the current file is unconfirmed.

title: UNESCO AI competency framework for teachers
author: UNESCO
summary: Fifteen teacher competencies across five dimensions and three progression levels - acquire, deepen, create - intended as the basis for national teacher-training programmes on AI rather than for individual study.
who_for: Teacher educators, ministry staff and school leaders designing AI training or mapping existing CPD against a recognised standard. School and university level.
skip_if: Skip if you want anything practical for Monday - it is a competency map, not training, and contains no prompts or activities. Skip if you already follow a national framework such as the UK or Australian one.
notes: Published 2024. The page returned no content when I fetched it on 2026-08-21, so the framework details here come from search results and secondary summaries only - open it yourself before citing. It is the reference point that most other national frameworks cite.

title: Ethical guidelines on the use of AI and data in teaching and learning for educators (EU)
author: European Commission, Directorate-General for Education, Youth, Sport and Culture
summary: EU guidance for school teachers and leaders on using AI and data ethically, built around human agency, transparency, fairness, privacy and accountability, with guiding questions and school scenarios tied to the AI Act and GDPR.
who_for: School teachers and leaders in Europe who need guidance that lines up with the law they actually work under. Policy and classroom judgement.
skip_if: Skip if you want tool instructions - it never names a product. Skip if you are outside the EU; the legal hooks will not match your rules.
notes: First issued in 2022 and updated since to cover generative AI. I could not confirm the date of the current version from the landing page, so check which edition you are downloading - the 2022 text predates almost everything teachers now use.

title: Day of AI - free K-12 AI literacy curriculum (MIT RAISE)
author: MIT RAISE
summary: Free, open-licensed AI literacy units for every K-12 grade band with educator guides, teacher slides and student pages, covering what AI is, generative AI, bias, ethics and privacy, plus free online workshops for teachers.
who_for: School teachers of any subject who must teach students about AI, have no curriculum and no computer-science background. Teaching-students, school level.
skip_if: Skip if you want to learn Claude yourself - this is student-facing and tool-neutral. Skip if you need something that fits one lesson; the units are designed as sequences across several sessions.
notes: MIT RAISE, non-commercial, aligned to the UNESCO student competency framework. Registration is needed for some materials. I checked the site listing and its own descriptions, not the lesson files, and no publication or revision date is shown per unit.

title: Empowering Education Leaders: a toolkit for safe, ethical and equitable AI integration
author: Office of Educational Technology, US Department of Education
summary: A 74-page toolkit in ten modules for district leaders: opportunities and risks, privacy and data security, civil rights and accessibility, evidence of impact, the instructional core, building an AI strategy and task force, AI literacy for staff, and updating policy.
who_for: US school and district leaders building an AI plan or an AI task force. Policy, not classroom practice.
skip_if: Skip if you are a classroom teacher - it is written for people who set district policy and buy software. Skip if you need current guidance; it is from October 2024 and predates most of what teachers now use daily.
notes: Possibly outdated - nearly two years old and tied to a 2023 executive order. The original page at tech.ed.gov/education-leaders-ai-toolkit returned no content when I fetched it on 2026-08-21, so this is the ERIC full-text copy of the same document. Metadata and summaries only; I did not read all 74 pages.
